land.text: the Louisiana territory that 'Spain had ceded ... back to France' in the (secret) Third Treaty of San Ildefonso, 1800

predecessors.note: Spain kept administering the colony until 30 November 1803, so the state exists in title from 1800 and in fact only from late 1803.

land.text: the Louisiana Purchase, 'nominally' 828,000 sq mi (2,140,000 km2); New Orleans turned over 20 December 1803, Upper Louisiana at St. Louis on 9-10 March 1804

capitals.name: New Orleans
capitals.note: The Louisiana Purchase page has the Spanish-to-French conveyance (30 November 1803) and the French-to-US turnover (20 December 1803) at New Orleans, but does not call it the capital; the French Louisiana page calls it a Creole cultural centre. The seat is inferred.

capitals.name: St. Louis
capitals.note: Upper Louisiana's handover to France and then the US took place at St. Louis on 9-10 March 1804 ('Three Flags Day'); the page does not call it a capital.

correction.text: the Louisiana territory ceded back to France in 1800 and later sold: the US 'nominally acquired a total of 828,000 sq mi (2,140,000 km2)'; French in title from 1800, Spanish-administered until 30 November 1803

keyframe_review.note: Cliopatria's 54,069 km2 shape for 1800-1802 holds about 78 cells of the state of Louisiana and 22 of Missouri, plus 66 cells of French Guiana and 5 of Guadeloupe: a bundle of fragments, not the territory the treaty named. The page area of 2.14 M km2 is about 40 times the shape (ratio 0.03), so the shape is wrong. French Guiana is covered by the french-colony-of-guiana dossier and Guadeloupe needs its own.

correction.text: for 1803 only: the whole Louisiana territory in French hands, the Spanish having conveyed it at New Orleans on 30 November 1803, until New Orleans was turned over to the US on 20 December 1803; Upper Louisiana follows as the 1804 keyframe

keyframe_review.note: Cliopatria's 107,958 km2 shape for 1803-1804 is the French Antilles and Guiana: 130 of 133 cells of Haiti, 251 of 252 of the Dominican Republic, all of Martinique and Guadeloupe and 66 of French Guiana, and no cell of Louisiana, the one thing the state held. Saint-Domingue was French until Haiti declared independence in 1804; the page says France withdrew its 7,000 surviving troops in November 1803. Those colonies need their own dossiers (notes).

correction.text: Upper Louisiana, still unhanded in early 1804: 'Upper Louisiana passed from Spain to France and then to the U.S.' at St. Louis on 9-10 March 1804; the lower colony (the state of Louisiana) went to the US on 20 December 1803

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe for 1804 (to March). The split into lower and upper Louisiana is the researcher's reading of the page's two ceremonies (New Orleans 20 December 1803, St. Louis 9-10 March 1804); the sale treaty (30 April 1803) conveyed the whole territory in law.

region.text: the Louisiana territory that Spain 'had ceded ... back to France'

ledger.note: 1800: Spain cedes Louisiana back to France in the secret Third Treaty of San Ildefonso. 'Spain had ceded the Louisiana territory back to France'; the French Louisiana page says France 'regained it by treaty' in 1800. Both pages give the year only; the Treaty of Aranjuez (1801) called it a 'restoration', not a retrocession.

region.text: New Orleans and the lower colony, still administered by Spain

ledger.note: 1800: Spain keeps the colony. The page dates the French takeover of 'the colonial lands and their administration' to 30 November 1803, so until then Spanish officials ran what France held in title; used here as an occupation so the map shows French title and Spanish control separately.

region.text: Upper Louisiana, still administered by Spain

ledger.note: 1800: Upper Louisiana stays Spanish-run too; it passes 'from Spain to France' only on 9 March 1804 (Three Flags Day).

region.text: New Orleans and the lower colony, where 'Spanish officials formally conveyed the colonial lands and their administration to France'

ledger.note: 30 November 1803: Spain hands Louisiana to France at the Plaza de Armas (Jackson Square), New Orleans, 'ending Spanish administration'. Three weeks of actual French rule follow.

region.text: New Orleans, which France 'turned over to the U.S. at the Cabildo' with a flag-raising ceremony on 20 December 1803

ledger.note: 20 December 1803: France turns New Orleans over to the United States. The region (the state of Louisiana as the lower colony) is the researcher's reading; the treaty nominally conveyed all 2.14 M km2 in law. The sale treaty itself, signed 30 April 1803 in Paris and ratified by the US Senate on 20 October 1803, is the legal act.

region.text: Upper Louisiana, handed over at St. Louis

ledger.note: 9 March 1804: 'Upper Louisiana passed from Spain to France' at St. Louis (Three Flags Day, 9-10 March 1804); the page does not say Spanish administration there had ended earlier.

region.text: Upper Louisiana, handed to the US the next day

ledger.note: 10 March 1804: Upper Louisiana passes from France to the United States at St. Louis; 'Upper Louisiana passed from Spain to France and then to the U.S.'

1804: the last French Louisiana land goes to the United States. The French Louisiana page: 'While the political entity of French Louisiana ceased to exist' the language persisted. Haiti declared independence the same year, ending French Saint-Domingue, which Cliopatria also bundles into this row.

wars.name: Haitian Revolution
wars.outcome: French defeat: General Leclerc's expedition (December 1801) 'faltered amid resistance and disease', France withdrew its 7,000 surviving troops in November 1803, gave up its Western Hemisphere ambitions and sold Louisiana.
wars.note: The Louisiana Purchase page links the expedition to the sale; the war moved none of Louisiana's borders. The Saint-Domingue land is not in this dossier.

certainty.note: The Louisiana boundaries were disputed: Spain held the western limit to the Mississippi's west bank and New Orleans/St. Louis, the US claimed West Florida to the Perdido; the Adams-Onis Treaty of 1819 (ratified 1821) settled them. The territory's edges were never surveyed.

sources.title: French Louisiana
sources.note: Identity: colonial region from 1682, regained by treaty in 1800, sold in 1803, ceded to Spain and Britain in 1763; no infobox area.

sources.title: Louisiana Purchase
sources.note: San Ildefonso 1800, Aranjuez 1801, Leclerc 1801, treaty 30 April 1803, ratification 20 October 1803, transfers 30 November and 20 December 1803 and 9-10 March 1804, area 2.14 M km2.

notes: Cliopatria's French Louisiana (1800..1804) is a bundle: 1800-1802 fragments of Louisiana, Missouri, French Guiana and Guadeloupe; 1803-1804 Haiti, the Dominican Republic, Martinique, Guadeloupe and French Guiana. Both shapes are marked wrong and replaced by the Louisiana territory. The French Antilles and Guiana need their own dossiers: Saint-Domingue (to 1804), Guadeloupe, Martinique (neither is in polities.csv as a French row). French Guiana is covered by french-colony-of-guiana. The day of the Third Treaty of San Ildefonso and of the Aranjuez treaty are not on the pages opened and were left out. The 'occupation' by Spain 1800-1803 and the lower/upper split in 1800-1804 are the researcher's way of expressing title versus administration; a reviewer may prefer simply gain 1800 and loss 1803.
